extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners (and advanced students) interested in notice-and-comment and remedial doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework for when courts should invalidate or excuse agency rulemaking defects under the APA's notice-and-comment requirements and related doctrines (logical outgrowth; legislative vs. nonlegislative rules). Focuses on prejudice, functions of notice-and-comment, and proportionality of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §553 notice-and-comment procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 553 of the APA, an agency that wishes to adopt a rule must publish a '[g]eneral notice of proposed rule making' in the Federal Register, allow the public to comment, and 'incorporate in the rule[] adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory baseline from which courts have built further procedural obligations. Case law elaborates what counts as adequate notice, what the agency must disclose, and the consequences of skipping the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless-error standard for failure to provide notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical circuit rule is that 'the failure to provide notice and comment is harmless only where the agency’s mistake "clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, courts rarely find notice-and-comment errors harmless. Courts demand a showing that the error 'clearly had no bearing' on procedure or substance. Examples: Riverbend Farms v. Madigan and related circuit authority; Allina Health Servs. v. Sebelius reflects courts' hostility to harmless-error claims in §553 contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary functions to assess remedial prejudice: informational and participatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment rulemaking serves both informational and participatory functions: it assures agencies incorporate relevant information into decisionmaking and guarantees that members of the public have a voice in decisions that affect their lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A remedial inquiry should ask whether process deficiencies materially frustrated these values. Rather than a binary approach (arbitrary = fall, not arbitrary = stand), courts should ask how the defects affected information quality and public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational-prejudice inquiry (did lack of notice frustrate information function?)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating informational prejudice, ask: Did the agency tell the complaining party what it intended? Did it open lines of communication? What comments would the complaining party have submitted through the formal process that it didn’t or couldn’t in another setting? Did the agency already address those concerns? Were they the kinds of comments that might have made a difference?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether agencies solicited input by other means (listening sessions, workshops, informal meetings, leaks), whether these alternative channels conveyed the substance sufficiently, and whether the missing formal comment would likely have affected the agency’s substantive decision. Examples and authorities: agencies' extensive informal outreach, GAO findings, OIRA practice statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory-prejudice inquiry (did lack of notice deprive someone of participation right?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a person was 'blindsided' by adoption without notice and thereby deprived of a meaningful chance to participate — a deprivation that may carry intrinsic (dignitary) value apart from substantive impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider variation in the inherent value of process across challengers: individual small-business owners may suffer dignitary harm more readily than large public corporations. Also check whether the challenger actually participated in deliberations informally; if so, participatory objections are weakened. Consider whether the remedial objective (deterrence/private-attorney-general role) justifies invalidation despite lack of individual prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative channels and executive/agency commitments to public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing the need for stringent judicial remedies, courts should consider that agencies often secure public input outside formal notice-and-comment (e.g., leaks, press, listening sessions) and that executive orders and OIRA promote public comment even where not legally required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency has effectively signaled proposals (e.g., national media leaks), solicited substantive input informally, or later requested and responded to comments, courts should weigh these facts when deciding whether vacatur is necessary to vindicate notice-and-comment values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative vs. nonlegislative rule distinction (when notice-and-comment is required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires notice-and-comment only for 'legislative rules.' Agencies can issue nonlegislative rules—policy statements and interpretive rules—without formal procedures, but courts will treat them as legislative (and thus require notice-and-comment) when they are in substance legislative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests: policy statements are legislative when (1) they impose immediate, specific obligations on the regulated community and (2) the agency lacks genuine discretion to deviate; interpretive rules are legislative when they 'depart too far' from the statute or regulation they interpret (i.e., not tightly linguistically drawn). Authorities: Am. Bus. Ass’n v. United States; Paralyzed Veterans; 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(3)(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether a nonlegislative pronouncement is 'really' a legislative rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Because nonlegislative rules can affect private conduct and lead to enforcement, determine when those effects make a policy statement or interpretive rule effectively legislative (requiring notice-and-comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and agencies face uncertainty ('enshrouded in considerable smog'); invalidation for guessing wrong can be disproportionate when the agency reasonably believed it was issuing nonlegislative guidance. Consider whether regulated parties had been closely involved and whether the agency had provided prior rulemaking or public explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial proportionality: vacatur vs. holding error harmless or remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts typically vacate rules for notice-and-comment or logical-outgrowth violations, but vacatur can be an 'extravagant' or disproportionate remedy when (for example) the affected parties were actively involved, the issue had lengthy prior notice, or the agency provided substantial explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the severity of the procedural error, the extent of prior substantive engagement (e.g., extensive notice, media leaks, lengthy responses to criticism, OLC memos), and whether vacatur will disrupt governance unduly. Examples: DAPA (Texas v. United States) and GE v. EPA where courts vacated despite substantial prior engagement and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth / fair-notice standard for final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule must be a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule: the touchstone is fair notice — did the agency’s proposal give the public enough information to enable it to offer cogent comments?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine how specific notice must be (APA allows 'terms or substance' or a 'description of the subjects and issues involved'); courts balance preventing evasion with allowing agencies to refine proposals in response to comments. If a final rule is a surprising change that the public could not reasonably have anticipated, it risks invalidation. Cases: Long Island Care at Home v. Coke; United Steelworkers v. Marshall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice/showing required for logical-outgrowth failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts often presume vacatur for logical-outgrowth violations, a more nuanced approach asks whether the notice deficiency prevented the submission of incisive comments that might have changed the agency’s decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the record of comments (e.g., whether the issue was repeatedly raised in millions of comments), whether the agency provided general notice plus additional details via other channels, and whether challengers can identify what additional or different argument they would have made. Example: the 'waters of the United States' rulemaking where distance-based bright-line limits were argued to have been reasonably previewed by suggestions in the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that challengers show new arguments not previously presented informally
rubrics_metrics.description: When regulated entities have been informally involved in the rule’s development, courts resist holding the agency harmless unless challengers can show that they would have presented new arguments through formal comment that they had not already made informally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts worry that allowing agencies to avoid formal procedures while relying on informal consultation would eviscerate §553; thus they require challengers to identify unfamiliar arguments they would have made in formal comments. D.C. Circuit authority illustrates reluctance to accept harmlessness absent a showing that comments would have been different.
